lines.text: Press M on desktop, or tap the little light above your wrist in VR, to open your menu.
Left-handed? Settings → Menu moves the wrist light to your other wrist.
The Travel tab in your menu reaches all fourteen rooms with a soft fade. No walking required, though walking is lovely.
Looking for a friend? Menu → Aboard lists everyone, with a Go to button beside each name.
Sleep Mode makes everything darker and quieter, for you alone. Tap it again and your old settings come back exactly.
The room dimmers only change your own lights. Do dim with abandon.
Brightness is yours to choose and nobody else's. Slide it left for a sleepy room.
There are fourteen window views. Pick one just for yourself, or share it with the whole room.
Meteors, comets, an aurora and the odd maintenance drone pass by now and then. Set Sky events to Quiet to skip the chime.
The bar has twenty-two drinks, all named after something in space. Effects too lively? Settings → Comfort → Drink effects.
The Grow-jito and the Screwdwarf change your size for a little while. Order with care near low ceilings.
The Mezcal Wormhole takes you on a small tour of the station. Do hold on to your glass.
The koi in the garden love to be fed. In VR they may nibble your fingers. They mean well.
Pick flowers in the garden meadow; they grow back. The florist's bench turns them into bouquets and flower crowns.
Hold a flower crown above your head and let go: it stays on. Very fetching.
Paper lanterns from the florist's bench float beautifully on the koi pond.
The Atelier by the garden river has easels for painting. Press New easel if yours is taken.
The Library holds 1,500 classic books you can read right here. The card catalogue finds them for you.
Rumour has it a bookcase in the Library is not entirely a bookcase.
The Sleep Suite, the guest pods and the Studio have private voice. When the plaque says OCCUPIED, someone is having a quiet moment.
Pastel pens wait on the Library's pen board and on the pen trays in the Lounge and the Sleep Suite, for doodles and messages in the air.
The Spa has a hot tub, a cold plunge, an infinity pool, a sauna and a steam room. Towels are provided.
The Studio's barber chair comes with a full set of tools you can pick up and use. Gently, please.
The Home Cinema has an eight-metre screen and a popcorn machine. Room TVs elsewhere can show the same film.
Room TVs only play sound in the room you're in, and only if that room is ticked in your settings.
The pool table in the Games lounge turns into a party table with ten party games.
The Observation Dome has lying terraces and a planetarium projector. Ideal for doing nothing at all.
The Bridge clocks and the time-zone globe show where everyone aboard is waking up or going to sleep.
There's a porch swing in the garden. It sways all on its own, if you let it.
The glass lifts in the core stop at the Spa, the Dock, the Lounge, the Suite and the Dome.
Mirrors switch themselves off when you leave the room, so nobody stares at an empty one all night.
Settings marked “Just you” change only your own view and sound, and the station remembers them for your next visit.
Settings → Comfort → Furniture collision can make Beds, Seating or Tables walk-through, so you can lie inside a bed. Cups stay on tables.
Settings → Sound → ASMR sounds sets how loud the touchable objects are for you, whoever is holding them.
Settings → Sound → Ambience sets the ship's hum and each room's own sound, such as the Spa's water or the fire.
Settings → Room TV → Centre core (sound only) keeps the film playing in your ears while you wander the core.
Room TVs start switched off in the Library, ASMR Studio, Sleep Suite and Spa, so the quiet rooms stay quiet. Tick them in Room TV.
Rather not wear the wrist light? Settings → Menu → Show (VR) turns it off, and a wall panel opens everything instead.
Your menu tidies itself away when you walk about three metres from it. No need to close it first.
The big Station Settings panel moves to whichever is nearest: the Lounge, the Foyer, the Sleep Suite, the Cinema or the Dome.
In a private room, your menu's Room tab lets you lock the door and answer the intercom without leaving the bed.
Inside a private room, the plate sets Open, Locked or Resting. An empty room unlocks itself a few seconds after everyone leaves.
At a private room's door, press Ring. Inside, the intercom offers Let in, Talk or Not now.
Mirrors offer Off, Players, Full and See-through. Players shows only people and is the lightest on your computer.
The Sleep Suite has a mirror on the ceiling above the bed. Its switch is on the nightstand.
Room lights set to Night keep a soft glow on the floor so nobody trips. Each visit starts at Bright.
The meditation pod has three styles: Moonrise, Lantern and Star dome. The buttons are right of the door inside.
The ASMR Studio switches between Session and Midnight. The buttons are left of the door as you come in, and everyone sees the change.
On desktop, hold a bottle over a glass and hold Use to pour, then press Use with the glass to drink.
Had enough of a drink's effects? Water, the Astro-Naught, ends any drink and sobers you up a little.
In VR, tipsy drinks give a warm haze instead of a blurry, swaying screen. Gentler on the stomach.
Cinema popcorn comes Fresh, Salted, Sweet or Sweet & salty. In VR reach into your bucket to eat; on desktop, press Use.
In the sauna, tip the bucket over the stones (or press Use on desktop) for a burst of steam everyone can see and hear.
Reset buttons put a room's objects back for everyone, but they never take anything out of someone's hand.
At the party table you can raise or lower the table and hide the chairs just for yourself.
The pool table plays 8-ball, 9-ball, carom and three-cushion carom, chosen from the table menu.
Good evening. Or morning. Or whatever it is where you are; I keep all the clocks, but I don't judge.
Do mind the gap. There isn't one, but it's good practice.
The kettle is always on. I have stopped asking who keeps turning it off.
Should you require anything at all, I shall be right here. I am, after all, the building.
Shoes off in the Spa, please. I've only just had the floors done.
The smoke rings in the Nebula Club are rare. I'm told that makes them more impressive.
There is a pillow fort in the Sleep Suite. I have been asked not to call it structurally sound.
Space is very big. The lounge is very cosy. I recommend the lounge.
A gentle reminder that drinks with silly effects remain silly however many you have.
If you hear a soft chime, do look out of a window. Something lovely is passing by.
Welcome aboard. Your coat may go anywhere you like; there is, regrettably, no weather to keep off it.
I have polished every window on the station this morning. The universe looks marginally better for it.
Should you lose track of time aboard, do not worry. I have it written down somewhere. Several somewheres, in fact.
Tea is served whenever you would like it. In space, it is always a reasonable hour for tea.
I do not sleep, but I am a great admirer of those who do. Please carry on.
If anything aboard is not to your liking, do tell me. I shall be quietly disappointed in it on your behalf.
Visitors sometimes ask where the station ends and I begin. I prefer to keep a little mystery about it.
The view outside changes now and then. I take no credit. Well, a little credit.
Lie down wherever you like. Most of the furniture aboard was chosen with exactly that in mind.
The stars are very far away. I find that keeps them polite.
One does try to run a quiet station. The koi, I'm afraid, have never agreed to the arrangement.
I have counted the cushions aboard. Then someone moved one, and I have decided to stop counting.
Every room has its own little sound. The hum you hear everywhere else is simply me, thinking.
Should you find a room too bright, there are dimmers. Should you find it too dim, I apologise; I was setting a mood.
I am told the universe is expanding. I have checked the corridors and can confirm they have not.
I have no hands, which makes serving tea a creative exercise. The teapot and I have an understanding.
Good night, whenever your night happens to be. I shall keep an eye on the windows.
Please do not thank the lifts. They become insufferable.
I have been running this station for some time and have yet to find a single draught. Space is very good about that.
Should you need a moment to yourself, the private rooms are very discreet. So am I.
Cuddles are permitted in every room aboard. I have checked the regulations. I wrote them.
May I say, you look very well rested. Or you will, shortly. The beds here are rather insistent.
Time aboard is whatever you would like it to be. I simply keep the clocks honest about it.
I have dusted the stars. Only the near ones; the others are frankly too far.
Do feel free to put your feet up. I have had the footstools briefed.
The Library is quiet, the Spa is warm and the Lounge fire is lit. I believe that covers everything of importance.
Gravity aboard is set to normal. I have been asked to keep it that way, except at the bar.
Space is cold, dark and enormous. I find a good blanket helps with all three.
I do hope your journey was pleasant. The shuttle tells me it was, but it is terribly biased.
Hello again. Or hello for the first time. Either way I am delighted, and either way the kettle is warm.
Please excuse the view. It is always showing off.
I am not one to gossip, but the fireplace in the Lounge is a hologram. It is very sensitive about it.
Guests often ask if I get lonely. With this many cushions to keep plumped, I scarcely have the time.
The best seat aboard is the one you are in. I say that to everyone, and it is always true.
The koi are terribly polite. They will nibble a finger, but only if one is offered.
There is no rush aboard. I removed it some time ago, along with the alarm clocks.
I have reviewed today's schedule. It reads: be comfortable. I think we can manage that.
If you fall asleep mid-conversation, nobody aboard will mind. It is practically the house style.
On behalf of the whole station, thank you for visiting. The whole station is mostly me, but the sentiment stands.
Your room is ready. All fourteen of them, in fact. Do take your pick.
There is no weather outside to speak of. Inside, it is mild, with a strong chance of blankets.
The station has two lifts and a spiral stair. I am fond of all three, but the stair gets far less recognition.
Please do touch things. Most objects aboard make a pleasant little sound, and they do so love the attention.
I have been asked whether the station is haunted. It is not. It is merely very attentive.
Should you require silence, the Library will oblige. Should you require more silence, so shall I.
I find a cup of tea solves most things. The remainder are usually solved by a second cup.
I have arranged the stars for your viewing pleasure. Not personally, you understand. I merely chose the window.
Dress code aboard: whatever you are comfortable in. Pyjamas are not only accepted but quietly encouraged.
The sauna is hot, the plunge is cold and I am exactly room temperature. Somebody has to be.
The Observation Dome is excellent for looking at nothing in particular. I recommend it highly, and often.
Space travel is supposed to be exciting. I have done my very best to make sure it is not.
The tea is hot, the blankets are warm and the void is outside where it belongs. All is in order.
May I take your worries? I shall store them in the airlock and quietly misplace the key.
I am delighted you came. Most of my visitors are meteors, and they never stay for tea.
Do remember that every guest aboard is somebody's favourite person. Be gentle with them.
Some guests come for the Spa, some for the bar and some for the koi. Most stay for the sofas.
Nobody needs to do anything aboard. That is rather the point of the place.
Do stay as long as you like. The station has nowhere to be and neither, I hope, do you.
Your comfort is my only duty. My other duties are mostly clocks.
Sleeping guests will be left undisturbed. Snoring guests will also be left undisturbed, though I may hum along.
The bar staff are on duty around the clock. That is to say, whoever happens to be standing behind it.
One does not hurry in the steam room. One barely moves at all. That is the whole charm of it.
Ah, a new arrival. I shall try to appear calm about it, but I have been looking forward to this all day.
I tried to catch some fog this morning. I mist. Frightfully embarrassing for a building.
Why did the astronaut stay so calm? They needed space. I showed them to the Observation Dome; they've been up there since Tuesday.
The koi swam into the garden wall and said “Dam.” I've asked it not to swear in front of the lanterns.
I asked the kettle how it was feeling. It said it was just letting off steam.
Why don't planets ever queue properly? They keep going round in circles. Most irregular.
I told the Library a joke about paper. It was tearable.
The books in the Library are frightfully polite. They only speak when spoken to, and then only in chapters.
How does the moon cut its hair? Eclipse it. I offered it the Studio; it prefers to do it itself.
Why did the painting go to the Spa? It needed a little touch-up.
I meant to tell you a joke about the garden swing, but it keeps going back and forth on whether it's funny.
What's a koi's favourite instrument? The bass. I've asked it to keep the volume down.
Why did the lantern drift off across the pond? It was feeling a little light-headed.
The sauna and I don't get on. Every time we talk, things get rather heated.
I asked the stars if they'd like a cup of tea. They said they'd prefer something with a bit more twinkle.
Why was the comet so pleased with itself? It finally had a tail to tell.
I've been reading a book about anti-gravity. I simply can't put it down.
The infinity pool is lovely, but frankly I can't see where it's going with all this.
The beanbags in the Lounge have no ambition whatsoever. They simply sit there. I rather admire them.
What do you call a tea party in orbit? A gravi-tea. I'm frightfully sorry.
I was told to cut down on tea. I've switched to smaller cups. Progress is progress.
I asked a star if it was lonely. It said no, it was in a lovely constellation. I've been slightly jealous ever since.
Today's forecast: clear skies, a light breeze of nothing at all, and a chance of comets. Do bring a brolly anyway.
I tried to organise a race around the station. Everyone just orbited the start line. Not one person queued.
The teapot apologised to me this morning. It said it had been spouting nonsense. We're friends again.
The easels in the Atelier are terribly modest. Whenever anyone praises them, they just stand there.
What's the Atelier's favourite drink? Watercolour, with a splash of lemon.
I asked the planetarium projector for directions. It said they were written in the stars. Most unhelpful.
One of the Library's books has taken up stretching. It says its spine has never felt better.
Why won't the flower crown come off? It's grown rather attached.
The bouquets in the garden are ever so humble. They insist they're merely arranged.
I asked the cold plunge how it was getting on. It said “bit nippy, mustn't grumble.” Very British of it.
The steam room told me a secret. I'm afraid it was a bit vague. Everything is, in there.
Why won't the koi share its food? It's being a little shellfish. I've had a word.
What's a comet's favourite supper? Space-ghetti. I'll fetch my coat.
I tried to write a joke about the waterfall, but it just kept going.
I told the Bridge clocks a joke. Their timing was impeccable; mine, rather less so.
Which key does an astronaut press most? The space bar. They do keep asking where the actual bar is. The Lounge, if you please.
Ringed planets are my favourite. Lovely jewellery, and they never once complain about the weather.
The sun was offered a place at university, but it declined. It already had several million degrees.
The pillow fort has applied for planning permission. I've told it to join the queue.
Why did the lift win an award? It was always raising people's spirits.
The glass lifts are terribly honest. You can see right through them.
I asked a lift how its day was going. It said it had its ups and downs.
The secret bookcase has asked me not to mention it. So I shan't. Mention what? Exactly.
What did one window say to the other? “Lovely view today.” They say it every day. They're not wrong.
The meteors are frightfully punctual. They always arrive in showers, yet never once in the rain.
Teabags make terrible card players. They always end up in hot water.
Why did the biscuit see the doctor? It was feeling a bit crummy.
The maintenance drone outside always waves. I suspect it's just cleaning the windows, but I wave back.
Comets make dreadful secret agents. They always leave a trail.
The aurora is showing off again. I'd say something, but it's being terribly colourful about it.
What tea does a galaxy drink? Milky, naturally. Never black; black holes put it off.
I invited a black hole to tea once. It took every biscuit and gave nothing back. Shocking manners.
What did the pond say to the koi? Nothing. It just waved.
Why did the koi cross the pond? To reach the other side, I expect. Koi aren't terribly imaginative.
I asked the meadow flowers how they grow back so quickly. They said it's all about roots and not taking things personally.
The lanterns on the pond are very well read. They're always lit.
Why did the brush come to the Atelier? It wanted to make its mark.
The paintings are calm about everything. They have a gift for putting things in frame.
I told the cinema screen a joke. It just stared back blankly. Not so much as a flicker.
The popcorn machine gets terribly excited before every film. It simply pops off.
The pool table said it was feeling cue-rious. I told it to take a cushion and sit down.
The garden swing keeps saying it'll be right back. It always is. Then off it goes again.
I told the hot tub a secret. It's been bubbling about it all afternoon.
Why don't towels tell jokes? Their humour is far too dry. Rather like mine.
The barber chair has asked for a raise. I told it it gets one every time somebody sits down.
The hair dryer in the Studio is full of hot air. I'd tell it to its face, but it would only blow it off.
The shears in the Studio are terribly decisive. They always know exactly where to draw the line.
I asked a passing comet what it was up to. It said it was just passing through. It always is.
I'm not saying the station is cosy, but even the vacuum outside has asked to come in.
The welcome sign and I have a lot in common. We say the same thing to everyone, and we both mean it.
The Library asked its clock to tick more quietly. It's now simply taking its time.
Best day to visit the station? Sunday. Or Moonday. We're really not fussy.
I asked the planet outside to turn the other way. It said it would think about it. It's been rotating the idea ever since.
The kettle is the hardest-working appliance aboard. It's always in hot water so the rest of us needn't be.
Queuing for the lifts is a proud tradition aboard. Two lifts, nobody waiting. Still, one has standards.
I've been asked what the weather is like outside. Vacuum, mostly. Do wrap up warm.
What do you call a koi that's eaten far too much? A koi with a full tank.
The bubbles in the hot tub are frightfully cheerful. They're always on the rise.
Why did the planetarium get promoted? It was always looking up.
The Library's favourite tea is camomile. It says it helps it turn over a new leaf.
The garden bench has been sitting about all day. Honestly, some furniture.
The spiral stair is ever so supportive. It's always there to help you rise to the occasion.
The pavilion insists it isn't a building, it's a lifestyle. I've told it that's my line.
I'd tell you a joke about gravity, but it would only bring you down.
Why was the astronaut's tea so cold? They left it in space. Very easy to do. I've done it twice this week.
The Moon is going through a phase. Every month, without fail. I've stopped mentioning it; it seems happier that way.
I offered the Moon a biscuit. It said no thank you, it was quite full. Ask again in a fortnight, it said.
Why do astronauts make such good guests? They always bring their own atmosphere.
The ringed giant outside has never once been late. Mind you, it has had a few billion years' practice.
Why did the rocket do so well at school? It had excellent boosters.
A rocket once asked me for advice. I told it to take things one stage at a time. It's doing very well now.
Do rockets stop for afternoon tea? No, only for launch.
The countdown is the most British part of any rocket launch. Everyone waits patiently, in order, from ten.
A star once told me it was embarrassed. It went quite red, then rather giant. I've stopped asking it things.
Shooting stars would make dreadful cricketers. Terribly quick, but they never stay in for long.
Mercury always turns down a hot drink. It says it's quite close enough to the heat, thank you.
Venus is permanently under a cloud. I'd send it a get-well card, but the post takes months.
Jupiter has had the same storm for centuries. Even a British summer gives up eventually.
A year on Neptune lasts about 165 of ours. Imagine waiting that long for a birthday cake. I'd start queuing now.
Pluto was told it wasn't a planet any more. It took the news very well. Small, but terribly dignified.
A day on Venus is longer than its year. I've had Mondays like that.
Why did the planet go to bed early? It had been spinning all day.
The Moon follows us everywhere. I've decided to find it flattering.
I asked the Moon why it only ever shows us one face. It said the other side is its bad side.
Astronauts are marvellous at parties. They know how to make an entrance, and an even better re-entry.
What do astronauts read with their Sunday tea? The comet strips.
The satellites outside are terribly good listeners. They pick up on absolutely everything.
What do you call an astronaut who's always saying sorry? Apollo-getic. I'd never be like that. Sorry.
Meteors are terribly shy. The moment anyone notices them, they burn up and vanish.
Asteroids make poor dinner guests. They will keep crashing things.
A light-year measures distance, not time. I learned that the hard way, booking a very long holiday.
What do you call a comet that tells jokes? A comet-dian. Mostly one-liners, roughly every seventy-six years.
The universe is expanding. Nobody is quite sure why. I blame the biscuits.
The Sun never takes a holiday. It says it gets quite enough sun as it is.
I rang the ringed giant to say hello. It said it had plenty of rings already, thank you.
The craters on the Moon are only dimples. I told it so, and it positively beamed.
Moonlight is simply sunlight that's taken the scenic route. I approve of scenic routes.
What did the Sun say to the Moon? I'd lend you some light, but you'd only reflect on it.
Why are stars always tired in the morning? They've been out all night. Every night. For billions of years.
Every planet is a trifle at heart: a crust on top, something warm in the middle, and nobody sure what's at the bottom.
Stars are frightfully polite. Their light keeps calling on us long after they've left.
Telescopes are the most patient things in the universe. They'll wait years just to see something properly.
An orbit is simply falling over with great confidence and never quite landing. I've had evenings like that.
The station has been orbiting all day. Mustn't grumble; it's not as if it had anywhere else to be.
Space is mostly empty, which makes it a dreadful place to look for a lost sock.
The universe is nearly fourteen billion years old and still hasn't tidied its room.
Someone once said space has no atmosphere. They clearly never saw the Lounge on a quiet evening.
There's no weather in space, which leaves British guests with nothing to talk about. They manage. They discuss the lack of it.
I do miss rain. Not the getting wet, you understand. Just having something to complain about.
The solar wind is gusting to a million miles an hour today. I'd keep a firm hand on your hat.
The asteroid belt is the longest queue in the solar system. Nobody's quite sure what it's queuing for.
Comets are wonderfully well-mannered. They wait their turn, come round once in a while, and never push in.
I lost a biscuit in my tea this morning. I held a moment's silence, then poured another cup.
A rich tea biscuit went to the bank. It came out a plain tea biscuit. Times are hard.
What's a teapot's favourite dance? The cha-cha-chai.
The teapot is a dreadful gossip. Leave it long enough and it'll spill everything.
The tea and I agree on most things. Neither of us likes to be stirred unnecessarily.
I'm often asked how I take my tea. Seriously, mostly.
The shortbread doesn't mind being called short. It says it's well-rounded in every other way.
I tried dunking a biscuit in orbit once. The biscuit stayed put; the tea went for a little wander.
The custard creams and I have an understanding. They stay in the tin, and I stay polite about it.
A cosy jumper is just a hug that's learned to stay put.
Slippers are the most honest footwear. They never pretend they're going anywhere.
The koi asked for a bigger pond. I said they'd have to scale up first.
I asked one of the koi how it was finding life aboard. It said everything was going swimmingly.
The koi have no idea we're in space. I haven't the heart to tell them. They seem very content.
The koi are never in a rush. They simply go with the flow, and it's a lovely flow.
The meadow flowers are wonderful company, though they get a bit petal-ant if you leave them out of things.
The flower crowns are frightfully regal. They'd reign all day if the weather allowed.
Why don't flowers drive? They'd only put their petals to the metal.
The meadow is full of buds. Best buds, I'm told. They do everything together.
The garden flowers are very good at what they do. They really do grow on you.
Paper lanterns make hopeless secret keepers. Whatever they hold, they bring to light.
The stone lanterns are the most patient guests in the garden. They haven't moved a step all season.
The waterfall never learns. Every single drop falls for it.
What did the paint say to the canvas? Don't worry, I've got you covered.
The paints in the Atelier are terribly emotional. Leave them alone for a moment and they start to run.
I painted a self-portrait in the Atelier. It came out as a rather nice picture of a wall.
Painters never feel the chill in the Atelier. They always put on at least three coats.
Abstract art is marvellous. Nobody can tell if it's hung upside down, least of all the artist.
Library books are excellent at keeping secrets. They're always kept under cover.
The pastel pens on the pen board are terribly good at drawing attention.
Classic novels are like a good pot of tea: better the second time, and nobody minds if you nod off halfway.
The books in the Library are very well bound. You'll never get one to change its story.
The card catalogue knows where every single book lives. It just likes to be asked nicely.
The cold plunge has a frosty personality. Lovely once you get to know it, mind.
The towels in the Spa work ever so hard. By evening they're completely wiped out.
Hot tub etiquette: sit down, sigh, say "oh, that's lovely", and on no account discuss work.
The combs in the Studio have an awful lot of teeth and not a single bite.
The Studio mirror has seen some bold haircuts. It's very good about it. It simply reflects.
The combs are fiercely loyal. They'll stick with you through any tangle.
Popcorn is the bravest snack aboard. It faces the heat and comes out the other side, only slightly puffed.
Horror films are wasted on me. I'm the building; I already know what's behind every door.
The pool balls are very sociable. They're always knocking about together.
The party table used to be a pool table, and terribly reserved. Now it's the life of every evening.
The time-zone globe has confirmed it: it is always teatime somewhere.
The chart table knows exactly where we're going. It's simply too modest to say.
The lying terraces in the Dome are the only place aboard where lying down on the job is actively encouraged.
The Lounge sofas have one firm rule: whoever sits down first is not getting up again.
The Lounge cushions are the most easy-going things aboard. They take absolutely everything lying down.
Pillows hear everyone's last thought of the day. Not once have they repeated one. Proper professionals.
The pillows in the Sleep Suite have been feeling a little down lately. The feather ones especially.
The guest pods are rather small, but they're ever so good at fitting in.
Sleep Mode: when even the lights agree it's time to stop showing off.
I've never slept myself, but I'm told it's like Sleep Mode with fewer settings.
Yawning is catching. I once watched a single yawn travel round the entire Lounge like a very slow wave.
The smoke rings in the Nebula Club never say goodbye. They simply vanish into thin air. One admires the discretion.
The bar has twenty-two drinks named after things in space. Mine's a cup of tea, named after a cup of tea.
The cargo ship outside is very discreet. It never says what it's carrying, and I've never liked to ask.
The fireflies are the most cheerful visitors we get. They always light up the place.
The wrist menu is always close at hand. I'd call it handy, but I'm trying to cut down on puns.
People ask what the 9000 in my name stands for. It's how often I've said "lovely to see you". I meant every one.
I'd offer to take your coat, but after one of my jokes most guests prefer to fetch their own.
I've been told my jokes are out of this world. Usually while being shown the door.
Apologies in advance for the next joke. And the one after that. Possibly all of them.
I don't tell jokes for the laughter. I tell them for the groans. Groans are more honest.
This morning I bumped a cushion and said sorry. Then I said sorry for saying sorry. Then I put the kettle on.
If you're ever lost aboard, try looking apologetic. It won't help, but it's tradition. Then try the Travel tab.
The British have one great advantage in space. They've practised awkward silences for centuries.
How many butlers does it take to make a pot of tea? Just the one, and an enormous amount of pride.
Astronauts are the tidiest people I know. In zero gravity, if you don't put it away, it puts itself somewhere else.
Why did the satellite blush? It had been caught gazing at the Earth again. To be fair, it's a lovely planet.
The Bridge clocks all show different times, and every one of them is right. I find that very comforting.
What do you call a world made entirely of bad jokes? A pun-et. I've been asked to stop giving tours of it.
Comets are frightfully stylish. A bit of ice, a great deal of dust, and always a dramatic exit.
The Moon popped into the Spa for a facial. It left absolutely glowing, though to be fair it always does.
Every saucer secretly dreams of flying. I haven't the heart to tell them how far it is to the nearest alien.
The planetarium projector can show you the entire night sky. It also does the ceiling, but nobody ever asks.
Spacewalk advice: it's frightfully cold in the shade and roasting in the sun. Pack a cardigan for both.
The hardest part of running a space station? Finding somewhere to hang the washing.
The Sun has been shining for nearly five billion years. Still no one has thought to say thank you. Thank you, Sun.
The Observation Dome is excellent for stargazing. The stars, I'm told, have been gazing back for ages.
The ticking clock in the Library and I have agreed to disagree. It says it's late. I say it's cosy.
Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once on its axis, longer than the 225 days it needs to circle the Sun. Rather leisurely.
Venus spins the opposite way to most planets, so there the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us, so the Sun you see is always slightly out of date. I find that rather charming.
Moonlight is simply sunlight, borrowed and reflected. It takes just over a second to travel from the Moon to your eyes.
The Sun holds about 99.8 per cent of all the mass in our solar system. Everything else is, by comparison, a few crumbs.
Roughly 1.3 million Earths could fit inside the Sun, should anyone ever need the room.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than the whole Earth, and astronomers have been watching it for over 150 years.
Did you know Saturn is so light for its size that it is less dense than water? Given a large enough bath, it would float.
Saturn's famous rings are made mostly of water ice, in pieces ranging from tiny grains to chunks as big as a house.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest volcano known in the solar system, more than twice the height of Mount Everest.
On Mars the sky turns blue around the setting Sun, thanks to the way fine Martian dust scatters light.
A day on Mars is only about 40 minutes longer than a day on Earth. Mission teams call a Martian day a 'sol'.
Mars looks red because its dusty surface is rich in iron oxide, which is, more or less, rust.
Uranus is tipped over on its side, so it rolls around the Sun rather like a ball trundling across a lawn.
Remarkably, Neptune was found in 1846 thanks to mathematics: its position was predicted from the way it tugged on Uranus.
A year on Neptune lasts about 165 Earth years. It completed its first full orbit since its discovery only in 2011.
Neither Mercury nor Venus has a moon at all. Earth, I think, did rather well with ours.
Did you know Jupiter spins faster than any other planet? A day there lasts only about ten hours.
Did you know Jupiter's moon Ganymede is bigger than the planet Mercury? It is the largest moon in the solar system.
Saturn's moon Titan has rivers, lakes and seas, but they hold liquid methane and ethane rather than water.
Scientists think Jupiter's moon Europa hides a salty ocean beneath its ice, perhaps holding more water than all Earth's oceans.
Saturn's small moon Enceladus sends jets of icy spray into space from cracks near its south pole.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006. In 2015 the New Horizons probe spotted a large heart-shaped region on it.
A small fact for your tea break: the Moon is drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 centimetres a year.
On the Moon you would weigh about one-sixth of what you weigh on Earth. Hopping is strongly encouraged.
With no wind or rain on the Moon to wear them away, the footprints left by Apollo astronauts could last a very long time.
The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, which is why eclipses fit so neatly.
Seen from space, the Sun is essentially white. Our air scatters some of its blue light, giving it a yellowish look from the ground.
The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old and roughly halfway through its life. No need to rush your tea.
The core of the Sun reaches about 15 million degrees Celsius. I would let your tea cool rather more than that.
Each second the Sun turns about four million tonnes of its matter into energy. It has plenty to spare.
The Northern Lights appear when particles from the Sun meet gases high in our atmosphere. Oxygen gives the familiar green glow.
Our galaxy, the Milky Way, holds hundreds of billions of stars. The Sun is just one of them, some 26,000 light-years from the centre.
The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away, yet on a dark, clear night you can see it as a faint smudge.
A light-year measures distance, not time: about 9.5 trillion kilometres, the distance light travels in a year.
After the Sun, the nearest star to us is Proxima Centauri, a small red dwarf about 4.2 light-years away.
A sugar-cube-sized piece of a neutron star would weigh about a billion tonnes on Earth, much like a mountain.
Curiously, space is almost perfectly silent, because sound needs air, or some other material, to travel through.
Stars twinkle because their light is jostled by moving air in our atmosphere. Planets usually shine more steadily.
Most shooting stars are specks of space dust, many no bigger than a grain of sand, burning up high in our atmosphere.
The Perseid meteor shower each August comes from dust left behind by Comet Swift-Tuttle. Do bring a blanket.
Halley's Comet returns roughly every 76 years. Its next visit to the inner solar system is expected in 2061.
Voyager 1, launched in 1977, reached interstellar space in 2012. It carries a golden record of sounds and images from Earth.
The James Webb Space Telescope's main mirror is 6.5 metres across, made of 18 hexagonal segments with a thin coat of gold.
In 2019 astronomers revealed the first image of a black hole's shadow, made by linking radio telescopes around the world.
The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, judged from the faint afterglow of the Big Bang.
Here is a pleasant thought: much of the carbon and oxygen in your body was forged inside stars long ago.
The full moon nearest the autumn equinox is called the Harvest Moon, as it once lent farmers extra light in the evening.
A 'blue moon' is usually a second full moon in one calendar month, or the third of four in a season. It rarely looks blue.
Moonquakes are real. Instruments left by Apollo astronauts recorded thousands of them over several years.
Most scientists think the Moon formed from debris thrown out when a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth.
Venus is the hottest planet, though Mercury is closer to the Sun. Its thick carbon dioxide air traps heat like a heavy blanket.
The International Space Station orbits about 400 kilometres up, circling the Earth roughly every 90 minutes.
Because the ISS laps the planet so often, its crew can see around 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day.
The ISS measures about 109 metres from end to end, roughly the length of a football pitch.
At its best the ISS is the third brightest thing in the sky, after the Sun and the Moon. No telescope required.
People have lived aboard the ISS without a break since November 2000. That is a great deal of tidying up.
The ISS Cupola, built in Europe, has seven windows looking down on Earth. Surely the finest window seat there is.
Aboard the ISS, clocks keep Coordinated Universal Time, essentially Greenwich Mean Time. A thoroughly sensible choice.
The world's first space station, Salyut 1, was launched in 1971.
Skylab, America's first space station, was launched in 1973 and hosted three crews.
In microgravity the spine relaxes and stretches, so astronauts can grow up to about 3 per cent taller. It wears off back home.
To keep bones and muscles strong, ISS crew members exercise for about two hours every day.
Remarkably, the ISS can now recycle about 98 per cent of the water its crew brings aboard, including moisture from breath.
On the ISS, salt and pepper come as liquids: salt dissolved in water, pepper in oil, so no grains drift into the air vents.
Tortillas are popular in space because they make far fewer crumbs than bread. Floating crumbs are a genuine nuisance.
Astronauts on the ISS sleep in small crew cabins, zipped into sleeping bags fastened to the wall so they don't drift.
Many astronauts find food tastes milder in orbit, probably because fluids drift towards the head and leave them a bit stuffy.
I'm told that in weightlessness tears do not fall. They gather in a little ball of water around the eye until wiped away.
A candle flame in microgravity is round and blue, because without gravity hot air does not rise away from the flame.
Since 2016 the ISS has been fitted with LED lights that can shift colour through the day, helping crews keep a steady sleep rhythm.
Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space on 12 April 1961, circling Earth once on a flight lasting about 108 minutes.
Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in June 1963, spending almost three days in orbit aboard Vostok 6.
Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk in March 1965. He was also an artist, and took coloured pencils with him into orbit.
On Apollo 8 in December 1968, the crew photographed 'Earthrise', our blue planet rising over the grey Moon.
Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969, and Neil Armstrong became the first person to step onto its surface.
While his crewmates walked on the Moon, Apollo 11's Michael Collins waited in orbit above, circling the Moon alone.
Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972, across six Apollo landings.
Apollo 14 carried hundreds of tree seeds around the Moon. Back home they grew into 'Moon Trees', planted far and wide.
The famous 'Blue Marble' photograph of the whole, sunlit Earth was taken by the Apollo 17 crew in December 1972.
In 1962 John Glenn became the first American to eat in orbit. His menu included applesauce squeezed from a tube.
Astronauts practise spacewalks underwater: NASA's Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory pool holds about 23 million litres.
Fruit flies were the first animals deliberately sent to space, aboard a rocket in 1947, and they came back alive.
Félicette, a small Parisian cat, flew to space on 18 October 1963. A bronze statue of her now sits in Strasbourg.
Ham the chimpanzee made a short spaceflight in January 1961, landed safely and later lived out his days in zoos.
In 1968 two tortoises flew round the Moon aboard the Soviet Zond 5, among the first animals to do so, and both came home safely.
Remarkably, in 2007 tiny tardigrades, also called water bears, survived exposure to open space on a European-backed experiment.
In 1973 two garden spiders, Arabella and Anita, learned to spin webs in weightlessness aboard Skylab.
In 1960 the dogs Belka and Strelka spent a day in orbit and came home safely, along with mice, insects and plants.
In 1994 small medaka fish became the first vertebrates to mate in orbit, aboard a Space Shuttle. Their eggs hatched in space.
Remarkably, the Soviet space dogs were mostly strays, chosen because life on the streets had made them hardy.
Black, green, white and oolong teas all come from one plant, Camellia sinensis. The difference lies in how the leaves are processed.
A small fact for your tea break: the tea plant is a relative of the garden camellia, and if left unpruned it grows into a tree.
Did you know Earl Grey takes its citrus perfume from bergamot, a fragrant orange grown mainly in southern Italy?
I'm told Britons drink an estimated 100 million cups of tea a day. Do have another.
Herbal 'teas' such as chamomile and peppermint contain no tea leaves. Strictly speaking, they are infusions.
A small fact for your tea break: rooibos comes from a South African shrub, not the tea plant, and is naturally caffeine-free.
Matcha is green tea ground into a fine powder. The plants are shaded for several weeks before harvest, deepening their green.
Afternoon tea is often credited to Anna, Duchess of Bedford, who in the 1840s wanted a little something before a late dinner.
Lapsang souchong owes its smoky flavour to leaves dried over pinewood fires. Rather like a campfire in a cup.
Tea was drunk in China for many centuries before it reached Britain in the 1600s.
A cup of tea usually holds less caffeine than a cup of brewed coffee, though both vary with strength and size.
A small fact for your tea break: coffee beans are not really beans, but the seeds of a small red fruit called a coffee cherry.
Most of the world's coffee comes from two species, arabica and robusta. Robusta usually carries more caffeine.
Arabica coffee is native mainly to the highlands of Ethiopia, where wild coffee plants still grow in the forests.
A popular legend says an Ethiopian goatherd named Kaldi found coffee after his goats grew frisky eating the berries.
In 17th-century England, a penny or so bought a seat at a coffee house, with news and talk. They were later called 'penny universities'.
The insurance market Lloyd's of London began in the 1680s in Edward Lloyd's coffee house, where merchants met for news.
Decaffeinated coffee is not entirely caffeine-free. A small amount usually remains in every cup.
In 2015 an espresso machine called ISSpresso brewed the first espresso aboard the International Space Station.
The word 'coffee' reached English in the late 1500s, by way of Dutch and Turkish, from the Arabic 'qahwa'.
Did you know old books can smell faintly of vanilla? As paper ages, its lignin breaks down into compounds including vanillin.
Johannes Gutenberg's printing press, developed around 1450, used movable metal type and changed reading for ever.
Paper was invented in China. Its development is traditionally credited to Cai Lun, a court official, around AD 105.
Japanese has a word, tsundoku, for acquiring books and letting them pile up unread. I could not possibly comment.
Penguin Books launched its first paperbacks in 1935, priced at sixpence to bring good books within everyone's reach.
'Bookworms' are quite real: the larvae of certain beetles, such as the furniture beetle, bore little tunnels through old books.
Medieval manuscripts were often written on parchment or vellum, made from carefully prepared animal skin.
Charles Dickens published many of his novels in monthly instalments, so readers waited eagerly for each new part.
The word 'library' comes from the Latin 'liber', meaning book, which originally meant the inner bark of a tree.
The British Library holds over 170 million items, from books and maps to stamps, patents and sound recordings.
Under legal deposit, a copy of every book published in the UK must be sent to the British Library.
The Bodleian Library in Oxford first opened to readers in 1602, and is one of the oldest libraries in Europe.
The Dewey Decimal Classification, still used to arrange books in many libraries, was first published in 1876.
Britain's Public Libraries Act of 1850 allowed towns to set up free public libraries for everyone.
Project Gutenberg began in 1971 and is often described as the oldest digital library.
Did you know koi are colourful varieties of the common carp, first bred by rice farmers in Japan in the early 1800s?
Contrary to what many assume, koi are not simply large goldfish. Both descend from carp, but they are different species.
With good care, pond koi can live for several decades. Patience suits them.
The Japanese name nishikigoi means, roughly, 'brocaded carp', after their richly patterned colours.
Koi can grow up to about 90 centimetres long, which makes for a rather grand pond.
Young sunflowers follow the Sun across the sky. Once mature, most face east, warming up in the morning light.
A sunflower head is made of hundreds of tiny florets, set in spirals that often follow the Fibonacci numbers.
The daisy's name comes from the Old English for 'day's eye', because the flower opens by day and closes at night.
I'm told hydrangeas can change colour with the soil: in acidic soil many turn blue, while in alkaline soil they turn pink.
Lavender belongs to the mint family, along with rosemary, sage and thyme.
Many flowers carry ultraviolet patterns that we cannot see but bees can, guiding them towards the nectar.
Lotus leaves stay clean by shedding water so well that the droplets roll off, carrying dirt away. It is called the lotus effect.
The giant Amazon waterlily, Victoria, has leaves that can grow to around 3 metres across.
A small fact for your tea break: botanically speaking, bananas count as berries, but strawberries do not.
Remarkably, some Great Basin bristlecone pines in California are more than 4,000 years old.
Britain's two native oak species support around 2,300 kinds of wildlife, from birds and bats to mosses and fungi.
A tree's growth rings can reveal its age, and their widths quietly record the good years and the lean ones.
If I may: that fresh smell after rain has a name, petrichor. Part of it comes from geosmin, made by bacteria in the soil.
I'm told robins often follow gardeners about, watching for worms turned up by the spade. A splendid working partnership.
Hanami is the Japanese custom of gathering beneath cherry trees to admire the blossom in spring.
Ultramarine blue was once made from lapis lazuli mined in what is now Afghanistan, and at times it cost more than gold.
Did you know Prussian blue was discovered by accident in Berlin in the early 1700s? It is often called the first modern synthetic pigment.
Egyptian blue, one of the oldest synthetic pigments, gives off invisible infrared light when lit, which helps experts find traces of it.
Tyrian purple was made from sea snails, and so many were needed that the dye stayed a luxury for centuries.
The collapsible metal paint tube, patented in 1841, made it far easier for artists to take their paints outdoors.
Oil paint is simply pigment ground into a drying oil, most often linseed oil, which comes from the flax plant.
Watercolour paint uses gum arabic as its binder, a natural gum from acacia trees.
Alexei Leonov's sketch of an orbital sunrise, drawn in coloured pencil in 1965, is often called the first artwork made in space.
In 2009 chemists at Oregon State University found a brand-new blue pigment, YInMn blue, quite by happy accident.
Isaac Newton arranged the colours of the spectrum in a circle, an early form of the colour wheel.
The sky looks blue because air scatters the short blue wavelengths of sunlight far more than the longer red ones.
Magenta has no single wavelength of its own. Your brain composes it from a mixture of red and blue light.
Most people see colour with three types of cone cell, sensitive to long, medium and short wavelengths: loosely, red, green and blue.
In English the fruit came first: 'orange' named the fruit long before it became the name of a colour.
Seen from an aeroplane, a rainbow can appear as a complete circle. From the ground, the Earth hides the lower part of it.
Most of us spend about a third of our lives asleep. Time very well spent, in my view.
Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night, according to health guidance.
Our most vivid dreams tend to come during REM sleep, when the eyes dart about beneath closed lids.
Did you know sea otters sometimes hold paws while resting on the water? It may help them stay together. I find that rather comforting.
Dolphins can rest one half of the brain at a time, keeping the other half alert enough to surface for air.
Koalas sleep or doze for around 18 hours a day, saving energy on their low-energy diet of eucalyptus leaves.
A NASA study of long-haul pilots found that a short planned nap, about 26 minutes on average, noticeably boosted alertness.
Remarkably, common swifts can stay airborne for about ten months without landing. Just how they sleep up there is still being studied.
I'm told cats sleep for around 12 to 16 hours a day. They have grasped something the rest of us are still learning.
Yawning really is contagious: seeing, hearing or even reading about a yawn can set one off. Pardon me.
For the record, the Great Wall of China is not visible to the naked eye from the Moon. It is far too narrow.
Contrary to popular belief, goldfish do not have a three-second memory. Studies show they can remember things for months.
We do not use only 10 per cent of our brains. Brain scans show activity across all of it, just not all at once.
Viking warriors did not wear horned helmets. That look largely comes from 19th-century costume and art.
The famous 'tongue map' is a myth. Every part of the tongue that has taste buds can detect all the basic tastes.
The tale of NASA spending millions on a space pen is a myth. The pen was privately developed, and both US and Soviet crews used it.
Bulls are not enraged by red. They see the colour poorly; it is the movement of the cape that draws them.
Lightning can certainly strike the same place twice. The Empire State Building is hit around 20 to 25 times a year.
Rest easy: the idea that people swallow spiders in their sleep is a myth. Spiders tend to avoid sleeping humans.
The far side of the Moon is not always dark. It gets as much sunlight as the near side; we simply never see it from Earth.
Our seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis, not our distance from the Sun. Earth is actually closest in January.
Astronauts on the ISS float not because gravity is absent, but because they are falling around Earth. Gravity there is about 90 per cent.
Snowflakes nearly always have six sides or six points, because of the way water molecules link together as they freeze.
Sealed honey keeps for a remarkably long time, thanks to its low water content and natural acidity.
Sea otters have a loose pouch of skin under each foreleg for storing food, and sometimes a favourite stone.
Did you know octopuses have three hearts and blue blood? Rather a lot of heart, I would say.
Owls cannot move their eyes in their sockets, so they turn their heads instead, up to about 270 degrees.
The word 'biscuit' comes, via French, from the Latin for 'twice cooked', after the way early biscuits were baked.
The first jigsaw puzzles, made in the 1760s, were maps glued onto wood and cut up to help children learn geography.
Honeybees tell their hive mates where to find flowers by performing a 'waggle dance'.
Emperor penguins huddle together through the Antarctic winter, taking turns on the chilly outer edge of the group.
Chocolate was a drink long before it was a bar. In ancient Mesoamerica, cacao was whisked into a frothy, often spicy, beverage.
